references.text: Isaiah's prophecy about Satan's fall from heaven: 'How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!' – a direct parallel to Jesus' vision of Satan falling from heaven like lightning.
Ezekiel's prophecy about the cherub being cast out from God's mountain due to pride, which is traditionally understood as a description of Satan's fall from his exalted position.
Revelation describes the war in heaven where Satan (the great dragon, the ancient serpent) was thrown down to earth – an eschatological parallel to Jesus' words about seeing Satan fall from heaven.
Satan is bound and cast into the abyss – a continuation of the theme of Satan's final fall and powerlessness, which Jesus sees beginning through the disciples' ministry.
Jesus says that 'the ruler of this world will be cast out' – a parallel to Satan's fall from heaven in Luke 10:18, where Satan's power is broken through Jesus' work.
A star that had fallen from heaven to earth, given the key to the bottomless pit – the image of a fall from heaven linked to demonic power.
The immediate context: the seventy returned with joy and reported that even the evil spirits were subject to them in Jesus' name – which gives rise to Jesus' statement about Satan's fall.
Jesus provides further context for the vision of Satan's fall by giving the disciples authority to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.
Satan has access to heaven and God's throne in the book of Job, but Jesus' words in Luke 10:18 show that this access is now coming to an end.
The Protoevangelium – the promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. Satan's fall from heaven is a fulfillment of this promise of victory over the evil one.
Jesus says that the ruler of this world has been judged – which corresponds with Satan's fall from heaven as a sign that his power has been broken.
Paul writes that Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them – a theological parallel to Satan's fall and loss of power.
